1:
The chapter turns from narrative to register, and Keil and Delitzsch explain in grammatical-historical terms why it exists at all. In the accounts of the southern and northern campaigns, the only kings named were those who had formed a league to make war on Israel, though the summaries at Joshua 10:40 and Joshua 11:17 state that Joshua had struck all the kings of both regions and taken their towns. To complete the record, a detailed list is given here — and not only of those Joshua defeated west of the Jordan, but of the two Amorite kings Moses had conquered, so that the whole of what Israel gained under God's help stands in one picture.

Matthew Henry reads that decision as an act of memory with a moral attached. The historian, before summing up the new conquests, first recites the older ones won in Moses's time, when Israel became master of the great kingdoms of Sihon and Og. His puritan-evangelical comment on it is unusually pointed: fresh mercies must not drown the remembrance of former mercies, nor may the glory of the church's present benefactors be allowed to eclipse the honour of those who went before. Joshua's achievements are great, and those under Moses are not to be forgotten on that account, since God was the same who wrought both.

Gill fixes the period — the kings struck in the days of Moses, as Jarchi remarks and as what follows makes plain — and Wesley glosses the plain on the east as the region east of Jordan called by that name in Deuteronomy 1:1. Clarke sets out the chapter's architecture in a sentence: kings east of Jordan conquered by Moses in the first six verses, and those west of it conquered by Joshua, thirty-one in number, through to the end. On the boundary itself he is specific. Arnon marked the whole southern limit of the land occupied beyond Jordan and the mountains of Hermon the northern; Arnon rises in the mountains of Gilead, runs a long way from north to south, and falls into the Dead Sea near the mouth of the Jordan.

Calvin says frankly that the chapter needs no lengthy exposition, since it only enumerates kings whose territories Israel took — two beyond the Jordan and thirty-one within Canaan. But he insists there is very good reason for setting the summary before the reader's eyes as a living picture of God's goodness, proving that the covenant with Abraham had been ratified and performed, in the words unto thy seed will I give this land at Genesis 12:7 and Genesis 15:18. From there his reformed comment turns to Joshua himself: he was eighty when he entered the land, and Calvin asks how there could be such vigour in an aged man, fit for so many wars and the fatigues of campaigning, unless heavenly power had supplied more than mortal strength. The unbroken run of victory, the success in all circumstances, the ease and speed with which cities fell — he takes these as evidence of the hand of God as plain as if it had appeared visibly.

Calvin adds a caution about the geography that is worth keeping through the rest of the chapter. Defining the countries by their boundaries was meant to display the divine power by showing their extent, but that display only works for readers who know where the places are. To dwell on names without that knowledge he calls vain curiosity. He allows that some sites deserve attention because Scripture mentions them often — the brook Jabbok, the district of Lebanon, the lake here called the Sea of Chinneroth — since a little attention helps the narrative; beyond that he is content to leave the work to those better skilled.
2:
Sihon is described by his capital and then by the reach of his rule. Gill notes that Heshbon was taken from the Moabites and made his chief city. Keil and Delitzsch work through the boundary clause by clause: Aroer on the Arnon is the ruin of Araayr on the northern bank of the Mojeb; the phrase rendered the middle of the river means from the town in the Arnon valley onward, that is the city of Moab known as Ar or Areopolis lying near Aroer, which is named as the exclusive starting point of the land Israel took while Aroer itself is included; half Gilead is the mountainous district south of the Jabbok; and the Jabbok meant is the upper Jabbok. They refer the whole to Numbers 21:24, Deuteronomy 2:36 and Deuteronomy 3:16.

Clarke gives the same limits in plainer form. Aroer stood on the western side of the Arnon, in the middle of the valley the river runs through; Sihon's kingdom reached from the Arnon and Aroer in the south to the Jabbok in the north. On the divided Gilead he explains the arithmetic: the mountains of Gilead ran from Hermon southwards toward the source of the Arnon, roughly the mid-point of Sihon's territory, so Sihon held the half of Gilead lying on the east of his lands. The Jabbok rises in those mountains, runs west into the Jordan, and bounds Sihon on the north and the Ammonites on the south.

Wesley takes up the odd phrase about the middle of the river and offers two reasons for it. It is not unusual even in his own day for a river to be divided between two lords, their jurisdictions meeting midstream. But there is a particular reason here: the city Ar, which was no part of Sihon's dominion but belonged to Moab under Deuteronomy 2:9, stood in the middle of the Arnon valley, so the middle of the river is properly named as Sihon's boundary on that side. On half Gilead he presses the Hebrew — the phrase does not mark where his rule began but describes the country he ruled, which started at Arnon, took in half of Gilead, and ended at the Jabbok, the other half of Gilead belonging to Og.
3:
The eastern side of the Jordan valley is added to Sihon's account, and Gill reads the plain as two things at once: the plains of Moab, which had belonged to Sihon's kingdom before Israel possessed them, and the plains of Jordan.

Keil and Delitzsch render the clause as a statement of what Sihon ruled — the eastern side of the Ghor between the Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea — and take the two directional phrases as fixing its corners: by the way to Beth-jeshimoth, and southward below the slopes of Pisgah, which is to say the north-eastern edge of the desert by the Dead Sea. They refer the reader to Deuteronomy 3:17, Numbers 21:15 and Numbers 27:12 for the terms.

Clarke identifies the waters. The sea of Chinneroth is Gennesareth, the same as the lake or sea of Tiberias. Over the Salt Sea he is less settled: the Hebrew has been understood by some as the sea of the city Melach, and he presses the difficulty in the form of a question — where is there anything that can be called a salt sea east of the lake of Gennesareth? Some, he reports, take the lake Asphaltites, called also the Dead Sea, the Sea of the Desert, the Sea of Sodom and the Salt Sea, to be meant. He places Beth-jeshimoth near the Dead Sea in the plains of Moab and Ashdoth-pisgah, on the usual supposition, at the foot of Mount Pisgah.

Wesley reads the phrase on the east as describing the plain rather than the sea of Chinneroth, which lay on the western border of Sihon's territory. The plains of Moab lay between the two seas and eastward of them both, which is exactly what the clause says once its subject is fixed. He adds an observation about the Salt Sea's older state: it was a famous plain, pleasant and fruitful, before it became a sea.

Read together, the four witnesses do different jobs on the same clause. Gill decides what the plain is, Keil and Delitzsch decide which side of the valley Sihon held, Clarke worries about which body of water the text means, and Wesley works out which noun the phrase on the east belongs to. The verse is short and every one of its terms has been contested.
4:
The register turns to the second Amorite king. Gill identifies him without ceremony — the country Og reigned over, another king of the Amorites struck by Israel in the days of Moses.

Keil and Delitzsch supply the sites and their modern traces. Og's two residences were Ashtaroth, probably to be seen in Tell Ashtereh, and Edrei, now Draa; they refer his territory to Deuteronomy 3:10 and Deuteronomy 3:13, and for the man himself to Deuteronomy 3:11, with Genesis 14:5 and Numbers 21:33 for the residences. Clarke sends the reader to the same places for Og and, on the phrase describing him as of the remnant of the giants, gives the Hebrew term Rephaim and points back to Genesis 14:5 and Deuteronomy 2:11.

Wesley explains the double residence as alternation — sometimes at the one city, sometimes at the other, both being royal mansions — and then delivers the line that Henry had also drawn from this detail: Israel made one grave serve the man who could not be content with one palace. Henry's fuller version supposes one seat may have been for summer and the other for winter, and turns the two palaces into a single burial with the same edge.

The two kings are set side by side deliberately. Sihon's territory was described by rivers and boundaries; Og's is described by where he lived, and the effect is to make the second king a person rather than a frontier before the record disposes of him.

The description of Og as of the remnant of the Rephaim is the one clause the register keeps from the older narrative, and Clarke's cross-references show why it needs them: the term has a history running back through Genesis 14:5, and the account of Og's defeat at Numbers 21:33 supplies what this verse assumes. A reader coming to the chapter cold learns only that a king of Bashan belonged to a remnant of giants and lived in two towns.

Keil and Delitzsch's identifications are of the kind that can be checked on the ground, and they offer them with the same tentativeness they use throughout — Ashtaroth probably to be seen in one mound, Edrei under a name still current. That is as far as the evidence takes them, and they do not push it further.
5:
Og's reach is given from the north downward, and the boundary meets Sihon's at half Gilead. Gill takes reigned in mount Hermon as rule over the people inhabiting the mountain, dwelling under it and adjacent to it, rather than possession of the peak itself.

Keil and Delitzsch quote the clause in full — Hermon, Salcah, all Bashan to the border of the Geshurites and the Maachathites, and half Gilead as far as Sihon's frontier — and then move directly into the two verses that follow, recording that these two kings were struck by Moses and referring the account to Numbers 21:21 and Numbers 32:33. They note that Moses gave the territory as a possession to the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half tribe of Manasseh.

Clarke fixes the extent from the other end. Bashan in the days of Moses and Joshua reached from the Jabbok in the south to the frontiers of the Geshurites and Maachathites in the north, at the foot of the mountains of Hermon. Between them the two commentators close the eastern territory: Sihon from Arnon to Jabbok, Og from Jabbok to Hermon, and the two halves of Gilead divided between them at the river.

What the verse accomplishes, placed where it is, is to make the eastern conquest a continuous block rather than two separate victories. The register has described both kingdoms by their limits, and those limits interlock — the border of Sihon king of Heshbon is named as the southern edge of Og's, so the reader can lay the two descriptions against each other and find no gap between them.

Gill's reading of the phrase about Hermon is a small but real interpretive decision. To reign in a mountain is not to hold a summit but to rule the people living on it and around it, and taking the clause that way turns a geographical marker into a statement about subjects. The same logic governs the rest of the verse: Salcah, Bashan and half Gilead are populated districts, and the borders of the Geshurites and Maachathites are named because those peoples were not part of what Og ruled.

Keil and Delitzsch's habit of quoting the next verses inside their comment on this one has a practical effect worth noting. It means their treatment of the eastern kings is continuous rather than verse-bound, and a reader looking for their note on the grant to Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh will find it here rather than where the grant is recorded.
6:
The two kings are disposed of in a single clause, and the land is given away in the next. Gill reads the smiting as done to the inhabitants of those kingdoms, struck with the edge of the sword and their countries possessed.

Wesley uses the verse for the reflection Henry had drawn at the head of the chapter, and puts it in almost the same words: fresh mercies must not drown the remembrance of former mercies, nor must the glory of the church's present instruments diminish the just honour of those who went before them. Joshua's services were confessedly great — and let those under Moses not be forgotten, since both together proclaim God the Alpha and Omega of his people's salvation.

Keil and Delitzsch add only the cross-references for the conquest and the grant. The distribution to Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh is recorded here because it belongs to the same transaction: the land east of Jordan was taken and assigned in Moses's lifetime, and the register is completing that account before it turns west.
7:
The second half of the chapter opens, and Henry treats the whole of it as a summary worth reading for what it proves rather than for the names it contains. He gives the limits first: the country lay between the Jordan on the east and the Mediterranean on the west, and ran from Baal-gad near Lebanon in the north to Halak on the Edomite border in the south. The boundaries are set out more fully in Numbers 34:2, but what stands here is enough, he says, to show that God had been as good as his word and had given Israel possession of all he promised through Moses — if only they would keep it.

Keil and Delitzsch give the same frontier in their own terms, from Baal-gad in the valley of Lebanon to the bald mountain going up toward Seir, referring to Joshua 11:17, and note that this is the land Joshua gave to the remaining tribes. Clarke observes that the phrase repeats what was said at that earlier verse.

Henry's second and third observations concern the country and its peoples. The land held mountains that were fruitful rather than craggy and barren, valleys covered with corn rather than boggy, plains with springs to water them, and even wildernesses — not empty, but less thickly settled, serving as foils to set off the richer parts. The nations in possession were descended from Canaan, and Henry notices that where Deuteronomy 7:1 counts seven, only six are named here, the Girgashites being absent. He offers two explanations without choosing: either they had been absorbed into one of the others, or, as the Jewish tradition has it, they withdrew into Africa at Israel's approach, seeing it was useless to contend, and so are not counted among the nations Joshua subdued.

His fourth point is the list itself, thirty-one kings, named and counted apparently in the order they were conquered — Jericho and Ai first, then Jerusalem and the southern confederacy, then the northern. From that Henry draws three conclusions. The land must have been remarkably fruitful to support so many kingdoms whose rulers preferred to crowd together rather than disperse into emptier country. The ambition of those kings was narrow, each content with one city and its villages, none apparently attempting to master the rest, though they combined when threatened. And the whole is a statement of God's goodness to Israel and an obligation laid on them, since thirty-one kingdoms were divided among nine tribes and a half. Henry then allocates them tribe by tribe — eight to Judah besides shares of Jerusalem and Geder, six to Benjamin, Hormah and part of Geder to Simeon, two to Ephraim, four to the half tribe of Manasseh, two to Asher, three to Zebulun, three to Naphtali, and Dor to Issachar.
8:
Before the names begin, the land is described by its kinds of ground and its peoples. Gill takes the six terms as a description of the whole of Canaan: parts hilly and mountainous, others vales and open fields, some dry and barren, others well watered, some lying north toward Lebanon and some south toward Seir.

Wesley corrects a likely misreading of one term. Wilderness here and elsewhere in Scripture does not mean land wholly desert and uninhabited but land thin of inhabitants, and he cites its use in 1 Kings 2:34 and Matthew 3:1. On the missing seventh nation he gives the same two options Henry gave — the Girgashites either incorporated with one of the other nations, or, by the Jewish tradition, withdrawn into Africa at Israel's approach, leaving their land to be possessed because they saw it was fruitless to contend.

Keil and Delitzsch pass straight from this verse into the roll and state the principle that governs it: the kings are given in the order in which they were defeated. They then anchor the first of them to the earlier narrative — Jericho at Joshua 6:1, Ai at Joshua 7:2, Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon at Joshua 10:3, Gezer at Joshua 10:33, Debir at Joshua 10:38 — and note that the kings named in the two verses after those are not mentioned by name in the tenth chapter at all.

That last observation is the useful one for reading the rest of the chapter. The list is not simply a recapitulation. Part of it recalls battles the book has already told, and part of it records conquests otherwise unreported, which is why so many of the coming names need identifying from the tribal allotments rather than from the narrative.

Gill's six-fold description covers the land by contrast rather than by survey — hill against vale, dry against watered, north against south — and the effect is to claim completeness without listing anything. The nations are handled the same way: six named, standing for the whole population Israel dispossessed.

Wesley's correction on the word wilderness matters for reading the rest of Scripture as much as this verse. A term that suggests emptiness in English described land that was merely thinly settled, and he gives three passages where the same word covers inhabited country. Applied here it changes the picture of Canaan the verse offers: not a fertile strip beside a desert, but a varied and populated land in which even the sparse regions held towns.
9:
The roll begins where the campaign began. Gill notes that Jericho was taken first and is therefore named first, and Clarke refers the reader to his notes on the earlier narrative for this and the verses following.

Ai is identified by its position beside Bethel, which is how the book introduced it. The two towns stand at the head of the list because they were the first two cities taken west of the Jordan, and their order preserves the order of the campaign rather than any ranking of importance.

The formula that runs through the rest of the chapter is set here — a city, and the word one — and it will be repeated thirty times without variation. The count is the point of the list, and the towns are named to make the count checkable.
10:
Jerusalem and Hebron follow, and Gill supplies the name the narrative had given the first of their kings: Adonizedek, one of the five kings taken and hanged after the southern battle.

Keil and Delitzsch treat this verse as the opening of a long unbroken block and run their identifications through it, naming in sequence the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, Eglon, Gezer, Debir, Geder, Hormah, Arad, Libnah, Adullam, Makkedah, Bethel, Tappuah, Hepher, Aphek, Lasharon, Madon and Hazor. Of these they mark Madon, Hazor, Shimron-meron and Achshaph as belonging to the northern confederacy of Joshua 11:1.

Two of the names in that run get particular attention. Geder they suggest may be the Gedor of the mountains of Judah at Joshua 15:58, preserved under the old name of Jedur. Hormah — the word means banning — lay in the south of Judah at Joshua 15:30 and was allotted to the Simeonites at Joshua 19:4; it was called Zephath by the Canaanites, as Judges 1:17 and Numbers 21:3 record, and stood on the southern slope of the mountains.

The pairing of Jerusalem with Hebron at the head of the southern group reflects the confederacy rather than the geography. Adonizedek had summoned the other four kings, and the list keeps them together in the order the battle produced.

Gill's identification of Adonizedek connects this entry to the narrative that produced it. The king of Jerusalem was one of five taken together and hanged, and the list records him as a single tally because the story has already been told. Naming him at all is a small departure from the register's manner, which elsewhere gives the city and the count and nothing more.

Keil and Delitzsch's method through this block is worth stating plainly, since it governs a dozen verses. They quote the roll in long stretches rather than verse by verse, then stop on the names that need work. Everything they pass over in silence is a town already placed in the earlier narrative or the tribal allotments; everything they pause on is a name that cannot be placed without an argument.

Hebron is named beside Jerusalem because the two belong to the same confederacy rather than because they lie together, and the register keeps the pair in the order the battle produced. Of the town itself it says only that its king was struck and counted.
11:
Jarmuth and Lachish are the next two of the southern five, and Gill names the first of their kings: Piram, a third of the five kings already noticed in the account of the battle.

The verse illustrates how the register works. Where the narrative has already given a king a name and a fate, the list supplies only the city and the tally mark; the identification has been made elsewhere, and repeating it here would slow a roll whose whole purpose is to be complete rather than discursive.

Jarmuth and Lachish both belonged to the southern group, and their kings were among the five Gill has been numbering — the same five whose end at the cave of Makkedah is recalled when that town reaches its own place in the list.
12:
Eglon closes the southern five, and Gill records both facts that matter: this was the last of the five kings, and his name was Debir.

Gezer is named beside him. The two are joined here because they were taken in sequence, Gezer having come into the account when its king came up to help Lachish and was struck with all his people.

The coincidence of names is worth noticing in passing: the king of Eglon bore the name Debir, and a city called Debir appears as the next entry in the list. They are unrelated, and the register gives no sign of finding the overlap awkward.

Gezer's inclusion is a reminder that the roll follows the campaign rather than the map. Keil and Delitzsch place its defeat at Joshua 10:33, after the five kings and before Debir, and the register keeps it in exactly that position.
13:
Debir and Geder are recorded. Gill identifies Debir as the place also called Kirjath-sepher, referring to his earlier treatment of it.

Geder is the more doubtful name, and Clarke offers the identification Keil and Delitzsch had also proposed: probably the same as the Gedor of Joshua 15:58, situated in the tribe of Judah. Neither commentator presses it further than probability.

Debir belongs to the southern campaign the book has narrated. Geder does not appear there at all, which makes it one of the first entries in the roll to record a conquest otherwise unreported.

Gill's cross-reference to Kirjath-sepher is the useful part of his note. A town that appears in the allotments under one name and in this list under another is exactly the kind of case where the register would otherwise leave a reader with an unplaceable king.
14:
Hormah and Arad are named together, and both belong to the far south. Gill notes that Hormah was formerly called Zephath.

Clarke adds the association that gives the name its force. Hormah is supposed to be the place where the Israelites were defeated by the Canaanites in the account at Numbers 14:45, and the name itself — he gives the Hebrew as meaning destruction — probably arose from that circumstance.

The town therefore enters this list carrying a memory of Israel's own reverse. A place named for a defeat suffered on the way in appears among the thirty-one taken on the way through, and the register makes nothing of the reversal beyond recording it.

Arad, named beside it, belongs to the same southern region and to the same period of Israel's approach from the wilderness.
15:
Libnah and Adullam follow. Gill places Libnah's fall in the same sweep as Makkedah and Debir, taken at the same time as the kings of those places and of others.

Adullam is the name Clarke stops on, and for a reason belonging to a later century. It was a city of the tribe of Judah, listed at Joshua 15:35; and in a cave at this place, he notes, David often hid himself during his persecution by Saul, as 1 Samuel 22:1 records.

Neither town figures by name in the narrative of the southern campaign as a separate engagement, so both are among the conquests this chapter preserves that the earlier account passed over.

Gill's grouping of Libnah with Makkedah and Debir reflects the sequence of the southern campaign rather than any statement in this verse, which gives the town and the tally and nothing else.
16:
Makkedah is the town with the cave, and Gill gives the whole episode in a clause: near to it five kings hid themselves, were taken out and hanged, and the city was afterwards taken by Joshua. It fell later to the lot of Judah.

Bethel is named beside it. The town had appeared already in the list by way of Ai, which the eighth verse located beside Bethel, so its own king is recorded here in his turn.

Makkedah's place in the roll is a small piece of order worth noticing. The five kings of the southern confederacy have already been counted one by one — Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, Eglon — and the town where they were finally taken is counted separately, as a kingdom in its own right rather than as the scene of their end.
17:
Tappuah raises a question of identity that neither witness settles. Gill reports that Jerome calls it Thaffu, notes that the name signifies an apple and may have come from a plenty of that fruit, and then lays out the difficulty: a city of this name fell to Judah, another place called Beth-tappuah stood nearby, and both are distinct from a further Tappuah on the border of Manasseh belonging to Ephraim — which some take to be the town meant here.

Clarke states the same problem more briefly and reaches the same non-conclusion. There were two places of the name, one in Judah at Joshua 15:34 and another in Ephraim on the borders of Manasseh, and which of the two is intended cannot be ascertained.

Hepher is the second name, and Clarke offers an identification he attributes rather than asserts: the same, according to Calmet, as Ophrah in the tribe of Benjamin at Joshua 18:23.

This verse is the first in the northern half of the roll where the identifications begin to fail, and the pattern set here holds through most of what follows. A name is given, one or two candidate sites are proposed from the tribal allotments, and the commentators decline to choose. That restraint is the honest response to a list which supplies a king and a city and nothing else, and it is worth registering before the harder cases arrive at Lasharon and Gilgal.

Gill's note on the meaning of the name is the kind of observation that survives in commentary because it is pleasant rather than because it settles anything. That Tappuah signifies an apple, and that the town may have been named from a plenty of that fruit, tells the reader nothing about which Tappuah is meant — and Gill offers it alongside the three candidate sites without pretending otherwise.

What the two witnesses agree on is the shape of the problem. There is a Tappuah in Judah and a Tappuah on the Ephraim-Manasseh border; both are real, both are attested in the allotment chapters, and the register gives no detail that would distinguish them. Clarke states the impasse and stops, which is the more useful response than a confident choice would be.
18:
Aphek is a name shared by several places, and Gill and Clarke both work through the candidates without agreeing on one. Gill lists an Aphekah in Judah, an Aphek on the Amorite border, and another in Asher, then reports that Adrichomius places this one in Issachar and identifies it with the site where the Philistines brought their armies against Israel in the days of Samuel and David, and where the king of Syria fought against Israel. He passes on Adrichomius's further claim that its ruins were still shown in the great plain, not far from Gilboa, east of Mount Carmel and five miles from Tabor.

Clarke's list overlaps but is not identical: one Aphek in Asher at Joshua 19:30, another in Judah, and a third in Syria at 1 Kings 20:26 and 2 Kings 13:17. Which of the first two is meant, he says, cannot be ascertained.

Lasharon is the harder case, and Clarke handles it as a grammatical question rather than a geographical one. There is no city of this name known. Some take the initial letter of the Hebrew as the sign of the genitive, and he notes that the Vulgate appears to have read it so, rendering the phrase as the king of Sharon. Sharon was a district rather than a city, celebrated in Scripture for its fertility at Isaiah 33:9 and Isaiah 35:2; some suppose it the same as the Saron near Lydda mentioned in Acts 9:35.

A king of a district rather than a town would be an exception in a list otherwise made of city-kings, which is presumably why the reading has never carried the day. The alternative is a city that has left no other trace at all.

Gill's report of Adrichomius is a good example of how a site gets attached to a name in this literature. A later writer places the town in Issachar, identifies it with the Aphek of two well-known battles, and adds a description of ruins in the great plain with distances from Gilboa, Carmel and Tabor. Gill passes all of it on as reported rather than as established, and Clarke, working from the same set of possibilities, declines to choose between the two nearest candidates.
19:
Madon and Hazor open the northern confederacy in the roll, and Gill supplies the name the narrative had given: the king of Madon was Jobab.

Both towns belong to the alliance that formed against Israel in the north, and Keil and Delitzsch group them with Shimron-meron and Achshaph as the four named at the head of that account.

The register has now worked through the south and turned north, keeping to the order of the campaigns. Hazor's king had been the one who sent to the others, and the city itself was the only one of the northern towns Joshua burned.

Gill supplies from the earlier narrative what the register omits. Jobab king of Madon was among those Hazor's king summoned, and the roll counts him here in the order the northern campaign produced.
20:
Shimron-meron and Achshaph complete the four kings of the northern league. Gill notes that Shimron-meron fell to the lot of Zebulun, and Clarke refers the identification back to his note on the earlier chapter.

Keil and Delitzsch use this stretch to give two of the fullest site descriptions in the chapter, reaching forward to the towns of the next verse. Taanach, allotted to the Manassites within the territory of Issachar and afterwards given to the Levites at Joshua 17:11 and Joshua 21:25, was never entirely wrested from the Canaanites, as Judges 1:27 records; they identify it with Tell Tanak, a flat hill sown with corn an hour and a quarter south-east of Lejun, the old name surviving in a small village at the south-eastern foot of the mound.

Megiddo receives the longer notice, and it is largely a list of what later happened there. Also allotted to Manasseh within Issachar and likewise not cleared of its Canaanites, it was fortified by Solomon at 1 Kings 9:15, and is known as the place where Ahaziah died at 2 Kings 9:27 and where Josiah was defeated and killed by Pharaoh Necho, as 2 Kings 23:29 and 2 Chronicles 35:20 tell it. Keil and Delitzsch note that Robinson showed the name preserved in the later Legio.

A town whose king is a single tally mark here becomes, in their hands, the place where two kings of Judah died. The register gives no sign of it, and the commentary supplies what the list omits.

Gill and Clarke handle the two names of this verse briefly, having treated them where the northern confederacy was first described. Shimron-meron's later allotment to Zebulun is the one new fact Gill supplies.

Their long note on Megiddo also carries a small methodological point. The identification rests on a name surviving through a Roman-era form into the modern topography, and Keil and Delitzsch credit the scholar who traced it rather than presenting the result as their own. That habit of attribution runs through their treatment of every contested site in this chapter, and it is what allows a reader to weigh the identifications separately from the commentary that reports them.

Taanach and Megiddo are named together here and again in the allotment chapters and in Judges 1:27, always as a pair and always with the same qualification attached: given to Manasseh, and not cleared of their inhabitants.
21:
Taanach and Megiddo are recorded, and Gill places the first in the tribe of Manasseh, passing on Jerome's report that in his own day it was a large village three miles from Legion on the plain of Esdraelon.

Clarke locates it more exactly for a reader with a map: a city in the half tribe of Manasseh west of Jordan, not far from the frontiers of Zebulun, at Joshua 17:11, and afterwards assigned to the Levites at Joshua 21:25.

Both towns pass into Levitical hands in the later distribution, which is one of the quieter connections between this chapter and the allotment chapters that follow it.

Jerome's report of a large village three miles from Legion is the kind of continuity these identifications depend on: a name surviving on the ground long enough for a later writer to attach it to the site.
22:
Kedesh and Jokneam are named, and both are places that keep their identity better than most in this list. Gill gives Kedesh to Naphtali and notes that it became one of the cities of refuge, situating it in upper Galilee on Mount Naphtali, four miles from Sephet, as many from Capernaum, and twenty from Tyre.

Keil and Delitzsch confirm the town as a Levitical city and city of refuge on the mountains of Naphtali, citing Joshua 19:37, Joshua 20:7 and Joshua 21:32, and add that it was the home of Barak at Judges 4:6, that it was conquered and depopulated by Tiglath-Pileser at 2 Kings 15:29, and that it remained a known place after the captivity. Their description of its condition in their own day is unusually concrete: an insignificant village still bearing the ancient name north-west of the lake of Huleh, or by another traveller's account a poor farmstead on a mound at the south-west end of a cultivated table-land, with hewn stones, relics of columns, sarcophagi and the ruins of two large buildings lying about, and an open prospect on every side.

Jokneam near Carmel they identify as a Levitical town in Zebulun at Joshua 19:11 and Joshua 21:34, and report the proposal of Van de Velde and Robinson that it survives in Tell Kaimn on the eastern side of the Wady el Milh. Clarke gives it the same tribal placing, at the foot of Mount Carmel near the river Belus, and notes that it too was given to the Levites.

Between them Gill and Keil and Delitzsch give Kedesh three distinct lives: a Canaanite royal city struck by Joshua, a Levitical town and city of refuge in Naphtali, and a ruined site with columns and sarcophagi lying about it. The register records only the first, and the rest is what the commentary brings to it.

Clarke's shorter treatment agrees on every point that matters, giving the town to Naphtali at Joshua 19:37 and noting its selection as a city of refuge at Joshua 20:7. That both towns in this verse later passed to the Levites is a coincidence of the list rather than a principle, but it is the second such pairing in a few verses.
23:
Dor and the king of the nations of Gilgal are the last two entries before the total, and both carry difficulties. Gill notes that Dor fell to Manasseh but was never possessed by them, as Taanach and Megiddo were not.

Clarke adds that the city fell to Manasseh at Joshua 17:11, reports Bochart's judgment that it was one of the oldest royal cities in Phoenicia, and records that the Canaanites held it, as Judges 1:27 says, and that Antiochus Sidetes later besieged it without taking it.

The second name is the puzzle. Keil and Delitzsch read the king as ruler of the Goyim, taking that as a proper name in the manner of Genesis 14:1, and identify the seat with a place named in the Onomasticon as six Roman miles north of Antipatris, surviving in the Moslem village of Jiljule — while noting the awkwardness that this village lies only two miles from the ancient Antipatris. Clarke reports a different line: that the phrase means the higher Galilee, called Galilee of the Gentiles or nations, so that the entry should be read as king of Galilee of the nations. He also mentions the suggestion that it is the country of which Tidal was king in Genesis 14:1, and concludes that the place is very uncertain and that commentators have made it more so by their conjectures.

Wesley adds the necessary negative. This is not the Gilgal where Joshua first lodged after crossing the Jordan, since there is no sign that place had either king or city; it is a city of the same name, probably in Galilee toward the sea, where various peoples might have resorted for trade, over whom this man was king.

Gill's observation that Dor fell to Manasseh but was never possessed by them belongs with what he said of Taanach and Megiddo, and the three together make a point the register does not: a king could be struck and his city counted among the thirty-one, and the town still remain in Canaanite hands for generations. Conquest and possession are not the same thing, and this chapter counts the first.
24:
Tirzah closes the roll, and the chapter ends by counting. Gill admits at once that no tribe is anywhere assigned it, then gathers what others have supposed: Adrichomius and Bunting place it in Manasseh, and Bunting describes it as a fair and beautiful city on a high and pleasant mountain, twenty-four miles north of Jerusalem. Gill records that Jeroboam had his royal seat there, as did his successors down to Omri, and passes on Lightfoot's suspicion that Shechem in Mount Ephraim and Tirzah may have been the same town — though he notes the reasoning cuts the other way, since Jeroboam appears to have moved his court between the erection of his idols and his son's death, which would argue some distance between the two. On the town's quality Gill has no doubt, and rests it on the name itself and on the allusion made to it elsewhere in Scripture.

Clarke agrees on its later standing — for a long time the capital of the kingdom of Israel and the residence of its kings, as 1 Kings 14:17 and 1 Kings 15:33 show — and says its site cannot be exactly ascertained, though it is supposed to have stood on a mountain some three leagues south of Samaria. Keil and Delitzsch are willing to be more definite, taking it for the present Talluza, an elevated and beautifully situated place of considerable size surrounded by olive groves, two hours north of Shechem.

On the total Clarke raises a textual point and then a historical one. The Septuagint gives twenty-nine rather than thirty-one and yet sets down only twenty-eight, confounding or omitting the kings of Bethel, Lasharon and Madon. As for so many kings in so small a territory, he takes it as evidence that their kingdoms were very small indeed — the kings of Bethel and Ai had perhaps twelve thousand subjects between them — and argues that in ancient times every village or town had its chief, independent of his neighbours and exercising regal power in his own district. He presses the point with examples from outside Scripture, observing that Britain was once divided into many kingdoms, that Julius Caesar found four kings in Kent alone, and that ancient Gaul and the many petty sovereignties of Germany are remains of the same pattern; so the numbers in Canaan need not surprise anyone.

Wesley draws the same conclusion and adds a purpose to it. Each was king only of one city or a small province belonging to it, which he takes to be the wise and singular providence of God, that they might be the more easily conquered. Then he turns, as Henry had, to what the number implies about the land: what a fruitful country Canaan must have been, to subsist so many kingdoms — and at this day, he writes, one of the most barren and despicable in the world, which he lays to the curse it lies under since its inhabitants rejected the Lord of glory.
